Notes: Evidence of a Jewish community living in a separate quarter of the city from the mid-18th century (year = midpoint approximation of 'mid-18th century'); earliest documented presence
Jews first settled in the 18th century in what became a special Jewish quarter (century only; midpoint 1750 used)

Local tradition: no Jew in Shumla until c.1780 when a pasha of Adrianople brought Jewish physician Hayyim Aaron Ashkenazi; families from Adrianople followed (later from Pravadi, Razgrad, Vidin); lived in an enclosed court ('ghetto') with a small synagogue
Traveller Barbié du Bocage: 38 Jewish families lived in the city in 1810 (Chifut mahalle on the Poroyna river); estimate based on families (x5)
American missionaries' report: city of 40,000 of whom 75% Turks, 20% Bulgarians and the rest Jews and Armenians (no separate Jewish figure); documents presence
The local synagogue was reconstructed in 1858
Synagogue construction completed and consecrated in 1860
Official Ottoman registration of real estate and population in 1865: Muslims 1076, Bulgarians 8108, Armenians 876, Jews 424 (book published 2015)
Alliance Israélite Universelle opened its first school in Bulgaria here, a girls' school, in 1869
Alliance Israélite Universelle boys' school built 1870, officially opened January 1871 (first Jewish boys' school in Bulgaria); girls' school three years later; trade school 1879
Jewish population of 1,100 in 1878
Romanian delegation to the Congress of Berlin stated a Jewish community of 1,000 souls lived in Shumen
According to historians about 743 Jews with more than 50 houses in 1880 (approximate)
Official census of the Principality of Bulgaria (1880/81) recorded 738 Jews in the city
January 1881 census (Sarafov 1882): Jews were 3.2% of Shumen's population; percentage only, no absolute figure given
In 1900 Shumen was listed among the 34 organized Jewish communities in the Principality of Bulgaria, numbering 1,200 souls
200 Jewish families in a total population of about 22,000; estimate based on families (x5); two Alliance schools with 120 boys and 110 girls
Jewish population numbered 1184 in 1905, 3.20% of the town's population
Jewish population of 1,200 in 1910
Formal Jewish community (obshtina) of Shumen created around 1923 according to surviving archival documents
At the outbreak of World War II the community numbered 616 souls
9 March 1943 deportation orders for 6,365 Bulgarian Jews; 53 Jews from Shumen included in this initial quota (subset; deportation not carried out)
Shumen's Jews were to be transported to Sofia on 10 March 1943 for deportation to occupied Poland; deportation not carried out

From May 1943 about 2000 Jews expelled from Sofia under the Law for the Protection of the Nation arrived in Shumen (influx of expellees, not the resident community; most returned to Sofia after 9 Sept 1944)
At the end of the war the Jewish community numbered 1,000 souls (likely includes Jews expelled from Sofia still in town)
As of 1 June 1948 there were 590 Jews in Shumen
As of 10 May 1949 only 88 Jews remained, due to mass emigration to Israel
Consistory census of 28 May 1949 counted 84 Jews in Shumen; most of the town's Jews emigrated to Israel in 1948-1949
Article states that in 1952 only about 500 Jews lived in the 'Jewish quarter' (conflicts with 1949 figures of 84-88)
Shumen Jewish community (obshtina) closed in 1964
Abandoned synagogue demolished in 1992
Small community of around 40 Jews affiliated to the local branch of the Shalom organization
Only a few Jewish families remain in Shumen (source publication year 2015)
2021 census (National Statistical Institute): 1,130 Jews in Bulgaria, of whom 11 in Shumen
In 2022, 40 Jews lived in Shumen
